words_to_read_new.meaning: mal- means bad + function means to work: to work badly
mal- means bad + nutrition means feeding: bad or poor feeding
mal- means badly + formed means shaped: badly shaped
mal- means bad or wrong + practice: bad or wrong professional work
mal- means badly + treat: to treat someone badly
mal- means poorly + nourished means fed: poorly fed
mal- means bad + -volence means wishing: bad feelings, wishing harm
mal- means badly + adjusted means fitted in: badly fitted in
mal- means bad + -ice means the state of: the state of wanting to do bad
mal- means badly + content means satisfied: a person who is never satisfied
mal- means poorly + adroit means skilful: not skilful, clumsy
mal- means bad + ware means software: bad software that harms a computer

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
Teacher script - read each line aloud as the word appears. Name every part, then fuse the parts into the meaning, the way sub (beneath) + marine (water) fuses into a vessel beneath the water.
**malfunction** - mal- means bad + function means to work: something that works badly. A breakdown!
**malnutrition** - mal- means bad + nutrition means feeding: bad or poor feeding, not enough good food.
**malformed** - mal- means badly + formed means shaped: shaped badly, not the way it should be.
**malpractice** - mal- means wrong + practice means professional work: wrong or careless work by a doctor or lawyer.
**maltreat** - mal- means badly + treat: to treat a person or animal badly.
**malnourished** - mal- means poorly + nourished means fed: poorly fed, not getting the food the body needs.
**malevolence** - mal- means bad + -volence means wishing: bad will, wishing harm on someone.
**maladjusted** - mal- means badly + adjusted means fitted in: badly fitted in, struggling to cope.
**malice** - mal- means bad + -ice means the state of: the state of wanting to do harm. Ill will. (You will meet -ice again on Wednesday!)
**malcontent** - mal- means badly + content means satisfied: someone who is badly satisfied, never happy.
**maladroit** - mal- means poorly + adroit means skilful: not skilful at all, clumsy.
**malware** - mal- means bad + ware means software: bad software made to harm your computer.
**Memory hook:** hear MAL, think BAD NEWS. Every mal word is something gone bad - a malfunction is a bad function, malnutrition is bad feeding. Students say MAL means bad, then whisper it to a partner.
sessions.extension: Once finished, add a suffix you know to one of your spelling words to make it longer, then explain the new meaning (malfunction -> malfunctioning). Stretch: use two different mal- words in one sentence that shows both bad meanings.

new_morph_activity.title: Morpheme sums for mal-
new_morph_activity.rule: Word building: I say the meaning sum, you build the mal- word on your whiteboard.
new_morph_activity.example: bad + to work = ?        bad + feeding = ?        badly + treat = ?        bad + software = ?
items: Build the word, then write mal- = bad beside it.
Boards up together on my signal.
new_morph_activity.footer: Stretch: invent a new mal- sum for a partner
new_morph_activity.notes:
ANSWER: malfunction, malnutrition, maltreat, malware. 1. SAY: I give you the meaning, you build the mal- word and write mal- means bad beside it. TIME: 3 minutes on whiteboards. 2. Read each sum aloud twice while students build. CIRCULATE: check mal- is bolted to a real base, not an invented one. 3. SCAN boards up together, pick two students to read a word and its meaning. TRAP: building a non-word like malhappy. Fix: say the word aloud - if we never say it, we do not build it; student swaps to a real base and rebuilds. STRETCH: build a mal- word with three parts, like malfunctioning. HELP: word bank in the board corner - malfunction, malnutrition, maltreat, malware.
---
Purpose: tachistoscope-style building from meanings locks mal- = bad before spelling. [You Do | Morpheme sums | Morphology]

grammar.header_notes: Five-minute finisher. Prepositions and prepositional phrases - day 1: what a preposition is. Whiteboards out before the I do.

i_do.title: What is a preposition?
i_do.rule: A preposition is a small word that tells us WHERE, WHEN, or in what DIRECTION something is. Examples: in, on, under, before, after, across.
i_do.example: The cat slept under the old table.
items: Test: does the word tell you where, when, or which way? Then it is a preposition.
Point to it: under tells us WHERE the cat slept.
i_do.routine: Eyes on me - watch the test
i_do.notes:
1. SAY: A preposition is a little word that tells us where, when, or in what direction. Watch: in, on, under, before, across. 2. MODEL: point at the example. Think aloud: under tells me WHERE the cat slept, so under is the preposition. 3. ASK: what does under tell us here? 5 sec, choral answer. EXPECT: where. TRAP: students point to a noun like table. Fix: student runs the test aloud - does table tell where, when or which way? No - so it is not the preposition; they point again.
---
Purpose: first exposure this week; anchor the where/when/direction test. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]

we_do.title: Find the preposition
we_do.rule: A preposition tells WHERE, WHEN or DIRECTION. Find the one word that does that job.
we_do.example: We walked across the wooden bridge.
items: Write the preposition on your board, boards up together.
Prove it: does it tell where, when or which way?
we_do.footer: Stem: It is a preposition because it tells ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: across (it tells the direction we walked). 1. SAY: Write the one word that tells where, when or which way. 15 sec, boards up together. 2. SCAN boards, back row first. 80%+ correct -> You do. Less -> re-model the test on a fresh sentence and re-ask with boards. 3. ASK: how do you know across is the preposition? EXPECT: it tells the direction. Stem: It is a preposition because it tells ...
---
Purpose: guided identification with the where/when/direction test. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]

new_morphology.meaning: the state, quality, or act of (makes nouns)

words_to_read_new.meaning: brave + -ery means the state of: the state of being brave - courage
rob + -ery means the act of: the act of robbing
mock + -ery means the act of: the act of mocking - making fun
treach + -ery means the act of: the act of betraying trust
flatter + -ery means the act of: insincere praise to please someone
forge + -ery means the act of: making a fake copy
bribe + -ery means the act of: paying someone to do wrong
drudge + -ery means the state of: dull, hard, boring work
slave + -ery means the state of: the state of being a slave
scene + -ery means a collection of: all the views around you
machine + -ery means a collection of: a group of machines working together
refine + -ery means a place for: a place where things are refined

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
Teacher script - read each line aloud as the word appears. Name every part, then fuse the parts into the meaning, the way sub (beneath) + marine (water) fuses into a vessel beneath the water. -ery turns an action or a quality into a thing you can name.
**bravery** - brave + -ery means the state of: the state of being brave. Courage!
**robbery** - rob + -ery means the act of: the act of robbing someone.
**mockery** - mock + -ery means the act of: the act of mocking, making fun of someone.
**treachery** - treach + -ery means the act of: the act of betraying someone who trusted you.
**flattery** - flatter + -ery means the act of: praising someone too much just to please them.
**forgery** - forge + -ery means the act of: making a fake copy to trick people.
**bribery** - bribe + -ery means the act of: paying someone to do something wrong.
**drudgery** - drudge + -ery means the state of: dull, hard, boring work that never ends.
**slavery** - slave + -ery means the state of: the cruel state of being owned as a slave.
**scenery** - scene + -ery means a collection of: all the scenes and views around you.
**machinery** - machine + -ery means a collection of: many machines working together.
**refinery** - refine + -ery means a place for: a place where oil or metal is refined.
**Memory hook:** -ery turns an action or a quality into a thing you can name. Brave becomes bravery, rob becomes robbery. Chant with me: add -ery, name the quality. Students say it, then whisper it to a partner.
sessions.extension: Once finished, turn one -ery word into a sentence that SHOWS its meaning, not just uses it. Reminder: showing the meaning means a reader could guess the word from your sentence. Stretch: join two ideas with a subordinate clause - one that starts with because, although or while and cannot stand alone.

new_morph_activity.notes:

CIRCULATE: the noun must be real and the label must fit - state, act, or collection. 3. SCAN workbooks up, pick two students to read a word and its label. TRAP: adding -ery to make a non-word like runery. Fix: say the word aloud - if we never say it, we do not build it; student swaps to a real base and rebuilds. STRETCH: build a -ery word with an extra part, like machineries or trickery. HELP: word bank in the board corner - robbery, bravery, mockery, scenery.
---
Purpose: word building fixes -ery as a noun-maker before spelling. [You Do | Word building | Morphology]

**justice** - just means fair + -ice means the state of: the state of being fair and right.
**service** - serv means to serve + -ice means the act of: the act or state of serving others.
**malice** - mal- means bad + -ice means the state of: the state of wanting to do harm. Ill will. (There is Monday's mal- again!)
**novice** - nov means new + -ice means the state of: someone in the state of being new. A beginner.
**cowardice** - coward + -ice means the quality of: the quality of being a coward, having no courage.
**notice** - not means to know + -ice: a sign that makes something known so people notice it.
**practice** - -ice makes it a noun: the doing of a skill over and over.
**apprentice** - -ice makes it a noun: a young learner in the state of being trained.
**crevice** - -ice makes it a noun: a narrow crack in rock or a wall.
**hospice** - -ice makes it a noun: a place that gives gentle care and rest.
**precipice** - -ice makes it a noun: the edge of a steep and dangerous cliff.
**office** - -ice makes it a noun: a place where work is done.
**Memory hook:** hear -ice at the end saying /iss/ (not ice cream), think the state or quality of. Just becomes justice, coward becomes cowardice. Whisper the frame: the state of being ___.
sessions.extension: Once finished, find and record an antonym for one -ice word (justice -> injustice). Stretch: add a prefix to flip the meaning, then use both words in one sentence that makes the difference clear.

new_morph_activity.title: Show the meaning of -ice
new_morph_activity.rule: Write a sentence that SHOWS an -ice word's meaning, not just uses it.
new_morph_activity.example: justice = the state of being fair.   Weak: There was justice.   Strong: The judge freed the innocent man, so justice was done.
items: Choose justice, service, malice or cowardice.
Write a sentence a reader could use to guess your word.
new_morph_activity.footer: Stretch: show two -ice words in one sentence
new_morph_activity.notes:
ANSWER: accept any sentence where the -ice word's meaning is visible (e.g. malice - She tripped him on purpose, out of pure malice). 1. SAY: Pick an -ice word and write a sentence that SHOWS its meaning, so a reader could guess the word. TIME: 4 minutes on whiteboards. 2. CIRCULATE: does the sentence reveal the meaning, or just use the word? Nudge weak ones with 'show me the fairness / the ill will'. 3. SCAN boards up, read two strong ones aloud and name why they work. TRAP: a sentence that hides the meaning (There was malice). Fix: student adds an action that shows it - what did malice make the person do? STRETCH: show two -ice words in one sentence. HELP: sentence starter 'The ___ was clear when ...' and the student finishes it.

i_do.title: More than one phrase
i_do.rule: A prepositional phrase = preposition + noun, and it tells where, when or how. A sentence can hold more than one.
i_do.example: Before lunch, we ran around the oval.
items: Before lunch tells WHEN; around the oval tells WHERE.
Two phrases, two jobs, in one sentence.
i_do.footer: You will hunt both phrases next
i_do.notes:
1. SAY: A prepositional phrase is a preposition plus the noun after it, and it tells where, when or how. A sentence can have more than one. 2. MODEL: point at Before lunch - that tells WHEN. Slide to around the oval - that tells WHERE. Two phrases in one sentence. TRAP: students find one and stop. Fix: student reads the sentence again and asks 'is there another where or when?'.

SCAN boards, back row first. 80%+ -> You do. Less -> find the first together, then ask 'is there another?' and re-scan. 3. ASK: what does each phrase tell us? EXPECT: After the storm - when; on the water - where. Stem: This phrase tells ...
